notes: Single included document, the LMU Academic Honesty Policy in the bulletin. Only items 5a-5d name AI; most other units are general integrity rules and procedure that apply to AI cases. Dropped three units that concern non-AI plagiarism or course-material distribution with no AI link (A: obtained via the Internet as one's own work; A: distributing course materials; B: appropriation of another's ideas). One UNCOVERED unit: mandatory instructor enforcement. Stance restrict (coder A) over delegates (coder B).

documents.title: Academic Integrity
documents.stance_why: Item 5a: "Employing AI to complete assignments without explicit permission from the instructor is considered academic dishonesty" and 5d bars AI in quizzes and exams "without express permission". AI is banned unless the instructor permits it, so the document sets a restrictive default. Coder A said restrict, coder B said delegates because permission rests with the instructor; the document does set the default itself and does not offer tiers or hand the whole decision to instructors, so restrict.
documents.summary: The LMU Academic Honesty Policy is a general integrity policy with one section on generative AI. It treats unpermitted AI use, unattributed AI content, AI fabrication and AI in assessments as dishonesty, then sets sanctions, procedures and appeals for all violations.

units.why: The statement of policy says "Violations of academic honesty undermine the fundamental educational mission" and "cannot be tolerated", giving the rationale and institution-level framework behind the AI provisions (P56).
units.anchor: Violations of academic honesty undermine the fundamental educational mission of the University
units.resolution_why: Only A coded the opening rationale. Source: 'Violations of academic honesty undermine the fundamental educational mission of the University and cannot be tolerated'. A rationale statement the codebook says to code; kept as P56.

units.why: "Students are responsible for understanding the standards of academic honesty" puts accountability on students for knowing the rules, including the AI rules in item 5; P29 (own what you submit) is the nearest accountability type.
units.anchor: Students are responsible for understanding the standards of academic honesty

units.why: The opening says "Students are responsible for contacting their instructor(s) before assignments are due" to resolve questions, which tells students to ask when unsure (P10); it applies to AI as part of academic honesty.
units.anchor: Students are responsible for contacting their instructor(s) before assignments are due
units.resolution_why: Both coders: P10, student, during-work, must. Source: 'Students are responsible for contacting their instructor(s) before assignments are due to proactively resolve any questions'. No disagreement; B's topic order differs only.

units.why: The definition of academic honesty, "acknowledge sources consistently and completely", sets the attribution principle behind the AI attribution rule; P24 is the nearest type.
units.anchor: acknowledge sources consistently and completely
units.resolution_why: Only A coded the honesty definition. Source: 'Academic honesty requires that all members ... acknowledge sources consistently and completely'. The general attribution principle behind the AI attribution rule; kept, though weaker than the AI-specific P24 unit.

units.why: Item 3c lists "Using resources and materials prohibited by the Instructor" as cheating, which lets instructors decide which resources (including AI) are banned; this is an instructor-set rule (P04).
units.anchor: Using resources and materials prohibited by the Instructor.

units.why: Item 3d says collaboration "that violates an Instructor's stated policies" is cheating, deferring to instructor-stated rules; the text does not mention AI so it fits P04 only as instructor discretion.
units.anchor: Collaboration on coursework that violates an Instructor's stated policies or instruction.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded item 3d. Source: 'Collaboration on coursework that violates an Instructor's stated policies or instruction' is cheating. AI is not named, but it makes instructor-stated rules binding; kept as P04 with weak AI link noted. B coded 3c ('resources prohibited by the Instructor') but not 3d.

units.why: The AI list is introduced as "may include, but are not limited to", so the examples are illustrative, not exhaustive. This scopes what counts as AI misuse; P61 (scope) is the nearest fit.
units.anchor: examples of academic dishonesty involving Generative AI may include, but are not limited to
units.resolution_why: Only B coded the framing sentence of the Generative AI section. Source: 'examples of academic dishonesty involving Generative AI may include, but are not limited to'. It states that the AI list is illustrative, a real scope statement; kept as P61.

units.why: Item 5a says "Employing AI to complete assignments without explicit permission from the instructor is considered academic dishonesty": AI is banned unless the instructor permits it, so this sets the fallback default (P06) for students; P36 also fits but the permission-default is the distinctive content.
units.anchor: Employing AI to complete assignments without explicit permission from the instructor
units.resolution_why: Both coders: P06, student, during-work, must-not, restrict. A left policy null, B normalized it. Source 5a reads 'Employing AI to complete assignments without explicit permission from the instructor is considered academic dishonesty'; the anchor states the default rule, so policy stays null and the misconduct label is coded in the next unit.

units.why: Same sentence classifies unpermitted AI use as "academic dishonesty", i.e. misconduct handled by the integrity process. Coded separately from P06 because it states the classification, not the default.
units.anchor: is considered academic dishonesty
units.policy: Employing AI to complete assignments without explicit permission from the instructor is considered academic dishonesty.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P36, student, when-misuse, informs but split on unit_stance (A restrict, B prohibit). Source 5a bans AI only without explicit instructor permission, so the position is restrict, not an outright prohibition. Kept A's verbatim policy, which does not go beyond the passage.

units.why: Item 5b says AI content "without proper attribution is considered plagiarism and is strictly forbidden", which demands attribution of AI output; best fits P24 (disclose/cite), since the rule is the attribution duty.
units.anchor: Using AI-generated content without proper attribution is considered plagiarism and is strictly forbidden.

units.why: Item 5b labels unattributed AI content "plagiarism", a misconduct classification under the integrity policy (P36).
units.anchor: considered plagiarism and is strictly forbidden
units.policy: Using AI-generated content without proper attribution is considered plagiarism.
units.resolution_why: Only A split item 5b into two units; B coded it once as P24. Source: 'Using AI-generated content without proper attribution is considered plagiarism and is strictly forbidden'. It states both an attribution duty (P24) and a misconduct classification (P36); two distinct rules, so the second unit is kept.

units.why: Item 5c: "Fabricating data or information using AI to deceive is a violation of academic integrity" forbids a specific AI misuse and classifies it as an integrity violation; it is coded P36 (unauthorized AI use treated as misconduct) because P19 covers having AI generate the work one submits, which this sentence does not say.
units.anchor: Fabricating data or information using AI to deceive is a violation of academic integrity.
units.resolution_why: A coded P19, B coded P36; actor, phase, modality and unit_stance agreed. The source sentence does not say AI produces the submitted work; it says fabricating data with AI to deceive 'is a violation of academic integrity', which is the misconduct classification in P36. Final P36.

units.why: Item 5d: "Using AI tools while taking a quiz, an exam, or other in-class or on-line assignment without express permission" is cheating, so AI is barred in assessments unless permitted (P22).
units.anchor: Using AI tools while taking a quiz, an exam, or other in-class

units.why: "The burden shall be upon the Instructor to provide evidence that it is more probable than not" sets the evidence standard for any misconduct allegation including AI misuse; fits P64 (fairness in allegations) as a student protection.
units.anchor: The burden shall be upon the Instructor to provide evidence
units.frag_end: committed the alleged academic honesty violation.

units.why: "A Student has the right to appeal the Instructor's decision" gives students a right to respond to allegations (P64).
units.anchor: A Student has the right to appeal the Instructor's decision

units.why: Students may appeal on listed grounds such as insufficient evidence or a disproportionate sanction. This is the right to respond and contest, P64.
units.anchor: The violation determination is not supported by substantial evidence.
units.policy: A student may appeal on grounds including that the determination is not supported by substantial evidence, that new relevant evidence exists, that the sanction is disproportionate, or that procedures were not followed.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded the appeal grounds. Source lists four grounds a student may appeal on (substantial evidence, new evidence, disproportionate sanction, procedure). A distinct rule from the right to appeal; kept as P64 with B's normalized policy, which matches the list.

units.why: "Instructors are expected to apply academic integrity standards consistently ... and pursue all cases of academic dishonesty" binds instructors to enforce, the opposite of declining to police (P60); no type covers a mandatory enforcement duty, so it is UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: pursue all cases of academic dishonesty
units.frag_end: pursue all cases of academic dishonesty.
units.policy: Instructors are expected to apply academic integrity standards consistently across all of their students in all of their classes and pursue all cases of academic dishonesty.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors must enforce integrity standards consistently and pursue all cases of dishonesty (mandatory enforcement duty).
units.resolution_why: A coded UNCOVERED, B coded P36; other codes agreed. Source: 'Instructors are expected to apply academic integrity standards consistently ... and pursue all cases of academic dishonesty'. This is a duty to enforce, the opposite of P60 (decline to police), and P36 covers classifying AI use as misconduct, not an enforcement duty. Kept UNCOVERED; the policy text is normalized to include both parts of the sentence.

units.why: The process section says an instructor "will inform the Student of the suspected academic dishonesty in an email" with evidence and a request to meet, so the student is heard before sanction; best fits P57 (talk with student before escalating).
units.anchor: will inform the Student of the suspected academic dishonesty in an email

units.why: The instructor meeting "provides an opportunity for the Instructor and the Student to discuss the suspected academic honesty violation, the evidence", the talk-before-escalating step (P57); distinct from the email notice unit.
units.anchor: an opportunity for the Instructor and the Student to discuss the suspected academic honesty violation
units.frag_end: any concerns the Student may have.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded the meeting step. Source: the meeting 'provides an opportunity for the Instructor and the Student to discuss the suspected academic honesty violation, the evidence'. A real procedural rule distinct from the email notice; kept as P57.

units.why: Sanctions listed include "a requirement to re-do the assignment; a reduced or failing grade", concrete penalties applicable to AI misuse stated in advance (P37).
units.anchor: a requirement to re-do the assignment; a reduced or failing grade on an assignment
units.frag_end: a reduced or failing grade in the course.

units.why: Higher sanctions ("Academic probation", "Suspension", "Dismissal") are stated in advance; a separate set of penalties from the instructor-imposed ones (P37).
units.anchor: Suspension from the University.
units.policy: Sanctions for violations may include academic probation, suspension and dismissal from the University.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this separate list of higher sanctions (B coded only the repeat-violation steps). Source: 'Sanctions for violations of the Academic Honesty Policy may include the following', then probation, suspension, dismissal. Real stated penalties, kept; policy changed from 'include' to 'may include' to match the source.

units.why: Escalation by offense: "The presumptive sanction for a second violation is suspension" and third is dismissal, a stated penalty escalation (P37).
units.anchor: The presumptive sanction for a second violation is suspension

units.why: Dismissal is the presumptive sanction for a third violation, a distinct step in the escalating penalties, P37.
units.anchor: The presumptive sanction for a third violation is dismissal from the University.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded the third-violation step (A coded second only). Source: 'The presumptive sanction for a third violation is dismissal from the University.' A distinct stated penalty; kept as P37.

units.why: "Factors to be considered in applying sanctions ... shall include the nature and severity of the violation and whether there is a pattern" describes how penalties are scaled; grouped with P37 as penalty rules.
units.anchor: nature and severity of the violation and whether there is a pattern of violations
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P37, admin, when-misuse but split on modality (A must, B informs). Source: sanction factors 'shall include the nature and severity of the violation and whether there is a pattern of violations', and the policy defines 'shall' as imperative. Final must.

units.why: "The Provost's office will provide an annual report ... detailing the number and type of violations" is a review/evidence mechanism on integrity cases, fitting P55 (gather evidence), though AI is not named.

units.frag_end: different areas of the LMU community
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P55, admin, over-time but split on modality (A must, B informs). Source: 'The Provost's office will provide an annual report', and the definitions say 'will' is imperative. Final must. AI is not named, but the report is the policy's evidence mechanism, so P55 is kept.

units.why: "Records will have a protected status, with access only as authorized" protects confidentiality of integrity case files (privacy); P50 (protect personal data) is the nearest type.
units.anchor: Records will have a protected status, with access only as authorized
